Title: Q. What is the best combat deck ?

Messages.Author: Rob Treasure
Messages.Body:
What is the best combat deck ?

With the rise in combat, I am interested to find out what people value as
the best combat deck they have made or played against and why? I was
intrigued by a post on the group a while back that classified all combat
decks as varying degrees of bruise and bleed. This of course is very true as
even a 'pure' combat deck has to plough through the minions to get to the
pool and it made me ponder which deck consistently comes out on top in
combat? Is it numbers or punch power that wins the day?

I realise the question is utterly situational and dependant on other decks,
players blah blah yada yada but is there one combat deck that you fear above
all others?

Rob.

Messages.Body:
On Tue, 15 May 2001 20:03:13 +0100, "Rob Treasure"
<R.Tre...@btinternet.com> wrote:

>What is the best combat deck ?

The one that gets things dead the best. =)

>With the rise in combat, I am interested to find out what people value as

>even a 'pure' combat deck has to plough through the minions to get to the
>pool and it made me ponder which deck consistently comes out on top in
>combat? Is it numbers or punch power that wins the day?

(IMO, your mileage may vary, etc.)

WARNING: THIS TURNED INTO A LONG RAMBLING STREAM-OF-THOUGHT POST.
THOSE WHO DO NOT LIKE READING SUCH, BUGGER OFF NOW.

It's not punch power. Hitting people for 7+ is not going to
consistently win. There simply aren't enough vampires with 6 blood on
them at any given point in time -- vamps tend to either have 1-4 or
8-11 blood on them.

It's not burnage. Burning guys is terribly complicated. Anathema is
nasty but not frightening, because of the amount of moving parts.
Trying to burn guys with the Tremere or Assamites is always good for a
giggle, but not for a win. And diablerie has its own inherent risks.

It's not sheer numbers of dead guys. The Gangrel can litter the
playing field with torporized vamps, but they don't win games any more
than anyone else... mostly because guys who get poked for 1 agg can
rescue themselves next turn, and putting in enough intercept to stop
all the rescues WHILE putting in enough combat to kill everything
WHILE putting in some way to oust your prey makes for a 150+ card
deck.

Well, what the hell is it, then? It's a combination of consistency
and "power at a point" (to steal a term from General A. Tacticus).

"Consistency": a good combat deck must screw up the opposing vampire
damn near every time it gets into combat. Something as simple as a
Disguised .44 can be ridiculously effective over the long-term. The
classic POT Rush deck does well on consistency - it has roughly 50+
cards that all, in some form or other, read "I hit you." The 'best'
deck in this department, however, is the one that consistently hits
the opposing vamp for right around 3-5 points of damage.

3 points is too much to be blithely ignored, except for maybe your
local Inner Circle member - and you should have the advantage in
numbers on him. But most vampires will be 8-caps or fewer, and most
of THOSE vampires will not have full blood. Consider Jost Werner, a
common target. Hitting him for 3 when he's full leaves him with 3
blood, and it's no longer quite so automatic to drop the Pulse on him.
And a Blood Doll is now more likely to be used to push blood TO him.
Did you torporize him? No -- but neither did you make yourself a
target to the rest of the table. If Lisette Vizquel drops a Torn
Signpost, Immortal Grapple, Pushing the Limit, and Claws on her first
combat, totally vaporizing some pathetic 4-cap, then people are going
to be a bit edgy about sitting near the deck in the future, and will
go out of their way to help its prey. =)

3-5 points is also a lot easier to reach for most decks. Animalism
can use Carrion Crows/Scorpion Sting for 4. Potence can drop a single
Undead Strength or Pushing the Limit. A simple Gas-Powered Chainsaw
tends to pay for itself quickly, and a .44 may lack immediate punch,
but its permanent defensive properties are well worth it. And adding
a little Celerity repairs its offense rapidly.

Few clans (actually, I can't think of one offhand) are incapable of
finding a way to consistently do 3 points of damage in combat. Even
the pitiful Toreador can use hands/Blur/Taste, for an extreme example.

"Power at a point": So you have a deck that can do 4 points per
combat every time. Your deck will still suck if you can't apply that
damage to the vampires YOU want. Going back to the example above,
suppose Jost Werner goes and Pulses himself as his first action. You
now have a target. If you can't hit the target, you can expect pretty
consistent bleeds of 3 at +1 stealth coming your way.

Classic POT Rush sometimes falls down pretty badly here, I'm afraid.
With its myriad 0-stealth actions and bleeds for 1, it doesn't have
any real way to guarantee that one specific vampire dies - so its
tactic is modified early on to "all vampires must die", under the
theory that if you kill them all, you definitely got the one you
wanted. This makes you a hell of a target, though, and can be a real
problem if people bring out more vamps than you can kill - or if you
are unable because of hand jam to kill -everything- fast enough. As
many have said, when it works, it works well - when it fails, it
explodes gloriously.

Adding stealth to a Rush sounds like a great idea, until you realize
how many card slots in your deck it takes to pull off - and what might
happen when people quit blocking you. Oops. But it -has- worked for
decks in the past, although I might be inclined to use it with
permanents as opposed to transients.

Intercept is, oddly enough, the premier option here - a well-built
intercept deck should certainly be able to get into combat with any
vampire it chooses (unless, of course, that vampire takes no actions,
in which case it can be reclassified under 'no threat'). But
Combining effective intercept with effective combat has been a puzzle
for as long as V:TES has been around. The Tzimisce are foremost here,
as they have two intercept disciplines (ANI/AUS) and two combat
disciplines (VIC/ANI) to draw from. But even they run into some
difficulty, since the best cards they have are transients and they'll
run out of those transients rapidly if they attempt to slaughter
everything.

>I realise the question is utterly situational and dependant on other decks,
>players blah blah yada yada but is there one combat deck that you fear above
>all others?

Seriously? =) The one that is the counter to my OWN combat. If I've
got Trap/Carrion Crows/Song of Serenity, I'll be scared of Potence.
If I've got guns, I'll be scared of the Animalism decks. And if I've
got Potence, I'll be scared of gun decks and Fortitude. (Gun decks
and Trap/CC/Song don't care about Fortitude, for the most part.
"They'll run out" is their battle cry.)

-- Derek

Glad I didn't ;-), as the stuff that followed sums up my opinion
pretty well. Some things I would like to add, emphasize or simply rant
about:

In other posts I read a lot about scary combat decks, but I think they
all focus on single effective combats. Vampire A vs. Vampire B is not
what the question is about, but - as Derek rightly points out -
consistency. Killing vampires doesn't win the game, although it may go
a long way towards this goal. Combat as such has to be seen as part of
the game environment. So the question asked by Rob has an easy, but I
guess rather unsatisfying answer: The best combat deck is the one that
handles the metagame best, which sees not only combat, but mostly
combat defense (S:CE and friends, Fortitude etc.). If I build a deck I
never include such a thing as "casual combat" - it's either dedicated
killing capacity or dedicated defense.
So what IS the best combat deck then? The one that handles the
metagame best, I said. Without the local and situational context, this
means: The one that does combat well in the most common metagame
types. At least down here good old honest Bleed is still the strategy
that wins most games, and the one everybody returns to if the
bloodshed gets too scary. Gangrel Potence is scary as hell, but
nothing that stops a fast bleeding predator. Tzimisce Intercept works,
but won't be effective against the most common combat defense, S:CE.
Rötschreck on top? Fine, one goes to torpor... As Derek rightly
pointed out: These combat monsters are deadly when they work, but
Lazverinus offing Gideon Fontaine with 6 aggravated is just overkill,
especially if there are 4 or 5 Friends Of Gideon just waiting for you
to run out of your valuable transient cards, be it intercept our
untap. So the best combat deck to me is the one that can handle these
situations best, and that IMHO is potence rush (Nosferatu or Brujah
flavour, Antitribu welcome - whichever you prefer). Okay, they rule or
explode, but they have the best chance to kill Joe Vampire in the
average metagame, and each and every one of them - which is more
important, since your forward momentum is to fill out the vacuum in
your prey's active region, metaphorically speaking.
I played many wicked combat decks in my (un)life as a V:TES player,
but every time I look at the metagame, rush looks more promising then
most other ideas. Why? Because while IG/Potence combat has problems
with Gangrel poke etc, all these decks which sometimes come along
during a metagame shift are not as good as Potence rush against the
bread and butter decks - sneaky bleed, politics... I found that
all-combat environments are quite easy to exploit - maybe because
people here don't build efficient combat decks, but I think because
most combat decks are effective in killing, but not effective in eiher
ousting or defending.

Interesting topic... Actually if I remember correctly the current
British metagame reads "Pack Fortitude or Die". Does that mean that
Tremere or Assamites will shine soon? If so, good, but then that would
mean that you are all too gentlemanly to deploy some real cheesy
weenie sneak & bleed or weenie politics. These should handle the
situation without ever touching a vampire - the minions will be rushed
and killed, but I don't see a Gangrel Potence deck quick enough to
destroy them all reliably.

Ah, my apologies for rambling as Derek did, without a proper warning
in the beginning.

Well, yada yada or not, I think it falls into 2 classes: "tournament"
combat decks and "local" combat decks. Atlanta sees a LOT of combat, but
you won't find us often rushing to the tournaments, much less to the finals,
with combat decks. Flipside, you won't see weenie monopotence pure-rush
Grapple decks, either, even in local games. And, oddly, you won't see
Majesty that much either, but that's a side effect of that "sleazy feeling"
that playing Presence gives.

In a tournament when I'm not playing combat (re: most every time), I
fear pure blind rush behind me, usually, since it will often take me down
and give my grandpredator 2 easy VPs, unless the rush deck is going
backwards also, giving my great-grand-preadator 3 VPs. I'm usually prepared
for a deck that can fight and oust, not a deck that just fights.

Anyway, to answer the "fear above all others" question, I'd say that
Animalism combat is among the worst to fight against. Carrion Crows being
*painfully* common after SW is non-strike damage flying all around, and
Trap/CarrionCrows/SongOfSerenity is just damn annoying. Furthermore,
Drawing out the Beast is such a gawdoffal hoser card for all-but-Caliean
long-range combat decks. As Derek often says, Animalism combat often puts
you in a "S:CE or die" situation.
That being said, if I'm playing S:CE, I don't mind Animalism combat, and
then I worry more about Immortal Grapple. I'm a big fan of Spirit's
Touch/Majesty for S:CE-at-long-range, a great get out of combat.
Put that together, and I think the "best" combat deck is the
Gangrel+Potence. DotB/IG/WHACK, with possible
SongOfSerenity/Trap/CarrionCrows stuff and/or prevention and/or making the
damage aggravated and possibly Disarming or Decapitating. Animalism/Potence
is bad enough, but "AND I prevent all of yours AND mine is agg" etc. make
the Gangrel one royal pain in the tuckus. Wynn is a particular pain of an
animal, because he's Old Dog that won't learn New Tricks, like simple
Obedience. =)

THAT being said, that doesn't mean I fear it most in a tournament; they
may or may not be able to oust people after building the world's most
kickass deck. But I sure fear for my vampires.

I similarly fear for my vamps when facing Assamites (anyone who's seen
Todd Bannister bring out Parnassus again and again DOES fear the Assamites),
but since DotB basically hoses[1] Assamite combat, I'd have to put Potent
Gangrel on top of THAT.

But that's back to the tournament/local separation. In a combat-heavy
metagame, you want the "trump combat," and I think the Potent Gangrel can
trump most all others. In a combat-light environment, all that
prevention/etc. could be better used card slots for say, speeding up the
deck, or those huge vamps could be replaced with "smaller and more" for
speed and more ousting actions.
I have to say I'm not really sure what the "best" light-combat
tournament "combat deck" is. Most of the assumptions (few-to-no maneuvers,
little-to-no prevention) just aren't true in the post-SW scene. I have yet
to personally see a combat deck win the finals in a tournament, so I'm
hardly one to judge what it takes.

[1] I may well revisit this assessment when FN comes out, if the Assamites
get some "set range" effect or nasty close range combat.

If you drop a Haven and all jump on them at once, usually you get them

intimidated into not taking actions you don't like.

Majesties in a deck - there are an awful lot of decks that don't block

decks carrying light combat these days to rely on SOLELY Majesty

(shrug) I made an extremely effective POT/PRE bruise-and-bleeder at
one point - I included the smallest pot/pre vamps I could find, a few
POT skill cards, Blood Dolls, the works. I left in about 8 Rush
actions (you only need to Rush your predator), and added about 8 Legal
Manipulations. I made room for this by cutting down the combat to
Torn Signpost/IG/Undead Strength -only-, and a bit less of it,
assuming that people will quit blocking after a certain point... which
is what happens, much like Hidden Lurker decks. After the first time
someone gets their head blown off by a lurking Watenda with a
Disguised Flamethrower, they go out of their WAY to not block as long
as Watenda is untapped. Max Hidden Lurker required in a deck: 6.
Tops. And you'll discard half of those anyway for hand jam.

Usually what happened is that I bled with a Legal, got blocked,
whacked someone for 5 (sometimes pressed and hit for an extra 3), then
didn't get blocked again for a couple turns. I saved combat for
'forward' mostly, but any time I ran out of Legals, I usually found
that I had one or two Rush actions in my hand, so I went and killed
something. Normally there was at least one vampire of my predator who
looked threatening, so they made a good target to cycle through the
combat and get a couple more Legals in hand.

Occasionally I got Deflected - no big deal since the bleed is at 0
stealth, and you can often convince your grandprey to either punch for
1, or if they have S:CE, you can cycle tons of cards and "forget" to
use the Immortal Grapple, letting them off the hook. The biggest
weakness was, interestingly, any sort of weenie bleed behind me - just
no way to kill them all. However, it could certainly move through its
prey -very- quickly; as one person put it, "well, it's either lose 3
pool or lose a minion, a real sucky choice".

<snip>

>> Combat as such has to be seen as part of
>> the game environment. So the question asked by Rob has an easy, but I
>> guess rather unsatisfying answer: The best combat deck is the one that
>> handles the metagame best, which sees not only combat, but mostly
>> combat defense (S:CE and friends, Fortitude etc.). If I build a deck I
>> never include such a thing as "casual combat" - it's either dedicated
>> killing capacity or dedicated defense.
>
>Do you define dedicated killing capacity as no wakes, no frills etc.?
>

Not really at this point, although my conclusion (rush being best IMO)
of course implies this. What I wanted to say: For me there are three
way to apporach the combat "threat" in V:tES - ignore, defend or
dominate. So either your deck is fast and cheap enough that it can
afford losing a few minions, it has dedicated defense (like maneuvers
plus S:CE or S:CE plus Fortitude) or it just tries to be better in
combat then everybody else. Which - and that was my point - usually is
easiest with rush, as it's (here it comes again) consistency in doing
the job is unsurpassed.

>> So what IS the best combat deck then? The one that handles the
>> metagame best, I said. Without the local and situational context, this
>> means: The one that does combat well in the most common metagame
>> types.
>
>I think this is one of the reasons that toolbox decks do well as they deal
>with a number of metagame twists and turns. I think toolbox with a powerful
>theme or backbone can kick a wide variety of ass.
>

It certainly can, although I obviously don't think that the best
combat deck is a toolbox deck. The thing you quoted - "all combat
decks are varying degrees of bruise and bleed" - works the other way
round as well: All bleed (politics, whatever) decks can be classified
as various degrees of bruise and something, because as every minion
can bleed for one, he will hit you for one. But that's philosophical,
or do you want me to answer: Dominate weenie sleaze is the best combat
deck, 'cause it can certainly fight, albeit not well, but it will win
you more games then any other deck. So to restate my opinion. I think
rush is best because it doesn't have to think about what its oponents
do. And it gets the job (combat) done more often then other combat
decks - not against other combat decks, but against most other
archetypes.

>At least down here good old honest Bleed is still the strategy
>> that wins most games, and the one everybody returns to if the
>> bloodshed gets too scary. Gangrel Potence is scary as hell, but
>> nothing that stops a fast bleeding predator. Tzimisce Intercept works,
>> but won't be effective against the most common combat defense, S:CE.
>> Rötschreck on top?
>
>Don't really rate Rotschreck decks myself. They eat master phase actions and
>are limited in kill potential to big vamp opponents.
>

Absolutely.

>Fine, one goes to torpor... As Derek rightly
>> pointed out: These combat monsters are deadly when they work, but
>> Lazverinus offing Gideon Fontaine with 6 aggravated is just overkill,
>> especially if there are 4 or 5 Friends Of Gideon just waiting for you
>> to run out of your valuable transient cards, be it intercept our
>> untap. So the best combat deck to me is the one that can handle these
>> situations best, and that IMHO is potence rush (Nosferatu or Brujah
>> flavour, Antitribu welcome - whichever you prefer). Okay, they rule or
>> explode, but they have the best chance to kill Joe Vampire in the
>> average metagame, and each and every one of them - which is more
>> important, since your forward momentum is to fill out the vacuum in
>> your prey's active region, metaphorically speaking.
>> I played many wicked combat decks in my (un)life as a V:TES player,
>> but every time I look at the metagame, rush looks more promising then
>> most other ideas. Why? Because while IG/Potence combat has problems
>> with Gangrel poke etc, all these decks which sometimes come along
>> during a metagame shift are not as good as Potence rush against the
>> bread and butter decks - sneaky bleed, politics...
>
>A good point. Pot rush does handle the staple dirt of S+B and Vote rather
>well. But you say it falls against poke and IMO hates 'intelligent' and
>consistant defence.
>

It's all about metagames. Gangrel poke I would classify as the worst
threat, but Gangrel poke decks are limited in almost any other game
situation. Tzmisce & Co., with their aggravated damage, are a
challenge, but I would still go and rush Meshenka with Agatha, smack
her good and proper, go to torpor and be rescued by her friend Hector.
He might be blocked, but he can still dish out some huge damage... In
the end it's a war of attrition, but I think Potence rush - which IMHO
makes best use of Taste Of Vitae (if not going to torpor, of course)
and uses mostly small minions - can still stay on top of these decks.
Maybe not win, but still...
The biggest thing in favour of rush is this: It forces the most
dramatic metagame shift. Certain Fortitude strategies, excessive
maneuvers and S:CE are one way, but against Rush this has to be really
extreme, while most other combat decks are held in check with fewer
sacrifices to your main strategy (in case of non-combat, that is).
Switching to poke combat decks is another, but a welcome one at that,
because these decks, as I stated, are really easily exploited by other
non-combat strategies.
One word about the "intelligent and consistant defence": You are
right, because rush combat is very simple to read, and this game
wouldn't be good if there'd be no defence against it. But as tried to
explain above: The preparations are huge, and intelligence only pays
off if everybody else takes rush into acount. At the end of the day
someone will exploit this, and the metagame shifts again. So maybe
here's one thing in favour of other combat decks - they are less
destabilizing and thus their window of opportunity is longer open...

bleed mayhem of old.
